stops.title: The journey out of Africa
stops.blurb: Small groups had left Africa before, but their lines mostly died out. Then, between about 60,000 and 50,000 years ago, one population moved out through southwest Asia and kept going. Genetic studies show that everyone alive today whose ancestry lies outside Africa descends mainly from this one movement, by a group that probably numbered only in the thousands.

links.label: Recent African origin of modern humans

stops.dateNote: Genetic and fossil evidence put the main dispersal between about 60,000 and 50,000 years ago.

stops.title: The giant animals vanish
stops.blurb: As modern humans spread across the world, many of its largest animals disappeared. One study counted 177 species of large mammals, of 10 kilograms or more, that died out between 132,000 and 1,000 years ago: 62 in South America and 43 in North America alone. It found the losses closely tied to where humans lived and spread, with at most a weak link to climate.
stops.debate: Climate change and humans both have broad support as causes of the extinctions, and their relative importance is still argued over.
stops.dateNote: The extinctions happened at different times on different continents. The study behind this stop covers 132,000 to 1,000 years ago.

stops.title: The oldest pictures and music
stops.blurb: On a cave ceiling in Sulawesi, Indonesia, someone painted three human-like figures around a wild pig. Mineral crusts that grew over the paint are at least 51,200 years old, which makes it the oldest known picture that tells a story. More than 35,000 years ago, people in what is now Germany were playing flutes carved from bird bone and mammoth ivory.
stops.dateNote: The date is a minimum age: the painting is older than the crust that covers it.

stops.title: Meeting the relatives
stops.blurb: The newcomers were not alone. Neanderthals had lived across Europe and western Asia for hundreds of thousands of years, and Denisovans further east. The groups met and had children together: people with ancestry outside Africa still carry about 2% Neanderthal DNA, from mixing dated to roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago. By about 40,000 years ago the Neanderthals were gone.
stops.dateNote: The mixing is dated from ancient genomes; the last Neanderthal sites date to about 40,000 years ago.

stops.title: Crossing the sea to Australia
stops.blurb: Even with seas far lower than today, no land bridge ever joined Asia to Australia and New Guinea, then a single continent called Sahul. People crossed from island to island over tens of kilometres of open water, which took boats or rafts and planning. Stone tools at Madjedbebe in northern Australia have been dated to 65,000 years ago; other researchers argue for about 50,000.
stops.debate: Clarkson and colleagues date the oldest tools at Madjedbebe to about 65,000 years ago. O'Connell and colleagues argue the tools may have moved down through the sand and that no site in Sahul is securely older than about 50,000 years.

stops.title: The ice age at its peak
stops.blurb: Between about 26,500 and 19,000 years ago the ice sheets reached their greatest size. Ice covered Canada and northern Europe. So much water was locked up in it that the sea stood about 125 metres lower than today. Britain was joined to Europe, Siberia to Alaska, and New Guinea to Australia. People lived through it on every continent they had reached.

stops.title: Wolves become dogs
stops.blurb: Dogs were the first domestic animal. Comparing the DNA of ancient people and dogs suggests that wolves became dogs in Siberia by about 23,000 years ago, perhaps while people and wolves were cut off there by the cold of the last ice age. Dogs then travelled with the first people into the Americas. By 11,000 years ago at least five distinct dog lineages had formed.
stops.debate: The Siberian origin and the date of about 23,000 years ago are inferred from how human and dog lineages split and moved. Where and when dogs were first domesticated is still argued over.

stops.title: Into the Americas
stops.blurb: The Americas were the last continents people reached. A camp at Monte Verde in Chile shows they were far to the south by about 14,500 years ago, probably after travelling down the Pacific coast. Fossil footprints at White Sands in New Mexico have been dated to between 23,000 and 21,000 years ago. If that holds, people arrived before the ice age peaked.
stops.debate: Whether people were in North America before about 16,000 years ago turns mostly on the White Sands footprints and how reliable their dates are.

stops.title: The first pots, made by foragers
stops.blurb: Pottery was invented by hunter-gatherers, not farmers. At Xianrendong Cave in southern China, pieces of pots date to 20,000 to 19,000 years ago, near the coldest part of the last ice age and more than 10,000 years before farming. In Japan, pots made by Jōmon foragers between about 15,000 and 11,800 years ago still carry burnt residues from cooking freshwater and marine foods.

stops.title: The ice age ends
stops.blurb: Layers of snow counted year by year in Greenland's ice record the end of the last ice age. About 14,700 years ago the climate warmed into a milder phase. Then came a cold spell, the Younger Dryas. At its end, 11,700 years ago, the ice records an abrupt shift: the start of the Holocene, the warm epoch in which all of farming and written history would unfold.
stops.dateNote: Ice-core dates count years before 2000 CE, so 11,700 years ago is about 9700 BCE.

stops.title: Bread before farming: the Natufians
stops.blurb: In the Levant, Natufian hunter-gatherers lived from about 14,600 to 11,700 years ago. At Shubayqa 1 in northeastern Jordan they built a half-sunken house with a floor of basalt flagstones. In its remains, archaeologists found charred crumbs of flat bread made from wild einkorn and club-rush tubers, 14,400 years old: bread was being made at least 4,000 years before farming began.

p: In a limestone cave called Leang Karampuang, on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, a painted scene shows human-like figures interacting with a pig. It was made at least 51,200 years ago. Its discoverers call it the earliest known surviving example of representational art, meaning a picture of something, and of telling a story in pictures.
It is not alone. A hunting scene in another cave in the same district, Leang Bulu' Sipong 4, is at least about 50,200 years old, and other caves there hold paintings in a similar style.

On the other side of Eurasia, in caves in the Swabian Jura of southwestern Germany, archaeologists found flutes made of bone and of ivory. They date from the time modern humans first settled Europe, more than 35,000 years ago. By then, the finders argue, music was already a well-established tradition.

Paint itself is hard to date. In limestone caves, though, water slowly lays down thin crusts of the mineral calcite, sometimes over a painting. The crust contains traces of uranium, which decays at a known rate, so the crust's age can be measured, and the painting beneath must be older.

The Sulawesi team used a newer version of the method, in which a laser samples the crust point by point and maps where the oldest layers lie. Measuring more precisely gave older minimum ages. The hunting scene, first dated to at least 43,900 years, turned out to be at least 4,040 years older than thought.
Every one of these dates is a minimum. The paintings could be much older than their crusts, and the method cannot say by how much.

For music, the evidence is thin because finds are so rare. Some researchers have argued that Neanderthals made music and musical instruments, but the flutes' finders say concrete evidence for that is lacking. Outside the Swabian caves, the earliest secure evidence for music comes from France and Austria and is younger than 30,000 years.

Pictures of people and animals arranged in a scene, and instruments that took skill to make and to play, are widely taken as signs of fully modern behaviour. The Sulawesi dates show that such picture-making goes back further in our species' history than had been recognised.

When modern humans spread across Europe and Asia, other kinds of human already lived there. Modern humans reached Europe more than 45,000 years ago and shared it with Neanderthals for several thousand years.

They did more than share it. Genomes from people who lived about 45,000 years ago at Ranis in Germany and Zlatý kůň in Czechia carry stretches of Neanderthal DNA. Those stretches trace back to a single period of mixing, dated to about 45,000 to 49,000 years ago, and it is the same mixing whose traces everyone with ancestry outside Africa carries today. The ancestors of all those people, it follows, were still one population at that time.

Further east lived the Denisovans. People met them too: Denisovan DNA survives in several East Asian populations and in Tibetans, who inherited from Denisovans a genetic adaptation to thin air at high altitude.

Denisovans are known directly only from fragmentary fossils. Their genomes have been read from a single site, Denisova Cave in Siberia. A jawbone found on the Tibetan Plateau, at least 160,000 years old, was identified as Denisovan from the proteins preserved in it, and showed that they lived far from Siberia and high in the mountains long before modern humans arrived.

The end of the Neanderthals is dated by radiocarbon. One study re-dated 40 sites from Russia to Spain with improved methods and found that the stone-tool tradition linked to Neanderthals ended between about 41,000 and 39,000 years ago.

Dating is hard here because radiocarbon reaches its limit at about 50,000 years. The same study found that Neanderthals disappeared at different times in different regions, and that they overlapped with modern humans in Europe for 2,600 to 5,400 years. The dates alone do not say why they disappeared.

The Ranis and Zlatý kůň people belonged to one small, isolated population, the earliest known branch to split from the lineage of all other people outside Africa. Human remains outside Africa older than 50,000 years seem to come from still other populations.
The other humans are gone, but not entirely. Part of their DNA lives on in people with ancestry outside Africa, and in Tibet a Denisovan inheritance helps people live at high altitude.

During the ice age, low seas joined Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania into one continent, Sahul, and joined much of island Southeast Asia to the mainland as Sunda. Between them lay Wallacea, a wide belt of islands that was never connected to either side. The gap between the two exposed shelves measured 1,000 to 1,500 kilometres, and getting through it by island hopping took several sea crossings.

No large land mammal had ever made the full crossing and settled. People did. Mitochondrial DNA, which is passed down from mothers, shows that the founders included at least nine or ten separate maternal lineages, and the founding group is estimated at somewhere above 72 to 400 people, probably many more. Numbers like that mean a planned settlement, in boats large enough to carry people and supplies on voyages of several days.

At Madjedbebe, a rock shelter in northern Australia, excavators found dense bands of artefacts: flaked stone tools, grinding stones, ground ochre and axes with ground edges. They dated the sand around the lowest band by optical dating, a method that measures how long ago grains of sand last saw sunlight, and concluded that people were there about 65,000 years ago.
Genetic clocks, which estimate dates from differences in the DNA of living people, give a second line of evidence.

The date. A second team argues that an age above 50,000 years for Madjedbebe is unlikely to be valid. The site lies in a sand sheet, and in tropical sand, rain, slow creep and above all termites can move objects downward, so that a tool ends up in sand older than itself. They point out that after decades of searching, Madjedbebe is the only site in Australia still claimed to be older than 50,000 years, and that genetic clocks and other sites put the first settlement of Sahul at about 48,000 to 50,000 years ago.
The excavators considered disturbance and rejected it, citing broken artefacts whose pieces fit back together within the same layer.
If the older date is right, people left Africa earlier than most evidence suggests, or an earlier group reached Australia and left no trace in the DNA of people living today.
People reached Sahul by sea tens of thousands of years before anyone settled the Americas or the remote Pacific islands. It took boats, planning and enough people to found a lasting population.
Dogs descend from grey wolves, and they are the only animal known to have joined human life during the ice age. The wolf population they came from appears to be extinct.

One reconstruction places the change in Siberia by about 23,000 years ago. At the coldest point of the last ice age, people and wolves there may have been cut off together from the rest of the world. Dogs then went with the first people across the Bering land bridge into the Americas, and spread with them through the continent from about 15,000 years ago.
By 11,000 years ago dogs had already split into at least five major lineages.

Two kinds of evidence are used. Bones are one: the oldest dog that researchers generally accept, from Bonn-Oberkassel in Germany, is about 15,000 years old. Older skulls have been put forward as dogs, but their DNA groups them with ancient wolves, not with any dog lineage.

The other is DNA. One team read the genomes of 27 ancient dogs, up to 10,900 years old, from Europe, the Near East and Siberia. All dogs turned out to share one ancestry, distinct from wolves living today. Another team compared the family trees of ancient dogs with those of ancient people in Siberia, Beringia and North America. The two sets of lineages split and moved in step, which is what points to Siberia and to the date.

The Siberian origin is an inference from how lineages divide, not a find: no securely identified dog remains of that age are known from Siberia, and a few possible ones still await genetic study. Where dogs were first domesticated, and how many times it happened, remain unresolved, as do the circumstances in which wolves and people first came together.

The dog was the first domesticated species, taken in by hunter-gatherers during the ice age. Its later history follows ours closely. Dogs moved with the first farmers into Europe, and with Arctic peoples across northern North America.

People reached the Americas from northeast Asia. Their ancestors lived in and around Beringia, the land that joined Siberia to Alaska when the sea was low. From there they moved south past the North American ice sheets and spread quickly: by about 14,500 years ago there was a camp at Monte Verde in southern Chile, some 15,000 kilometres from Alaska.

Three kinds of evidence fit together. Genomes of living and ancient Native Americans show a single founding population that separated from its Asian relatives more than 20,000 years ago. Archaeological sites give minimum dates for when people were present. At Monte Verde, wooden posts, hearths, tools and food remains were preserved under a peat bog. At White Sands in New Mexico, human footprints run through layers of an old lake shore. Seeds in those layers were radiocarbon dated to between 23,000 and 21,000 years ago, and a later study reached similar ages from pollen and from quartz grains, using two other methods.

For most of the twentieth century, the accepted view was "Clovis first": that the earliest Americans were big-game hunters who walked through a gap between the ice sheets about 13,000 years ago. Monte Verde and other sites are older than that, and the gap between the ice sheets probably opened too late, so many researchers now favour a route down the Pacific coast. White Sands pushes the date much further back, to the coldest part of the ice age. Critics questioned the first dates because water plants can take up old carbon and look older than they are. The second study answered that objection for many researchers, but not all, and few other sites of that age have been found.

The peopling of the Americas completed the spread of our species across the habitable continents. It also began a separation: for more than 15,000 years, people in the Americas and people in Africa, Asia and Europe built farms, cities and states with no knowledge of each other. Chapter 7 tells what happened when the two halves met again.
